entities.summary:
The Coliseum (also spelled Colosseum) in Rome is the largest ancient amphitheater ever built — an iconic symbol of the Roman Empire's engineering genius, military power, and cultural values, constructed under the Flavian emperors (Vespasian began construction circa 72 CE, completed by Titus 80 CE, with later additions by Domitian) to accommodate approximately 50,000-80,000 spectators for gladiatorial combat, venationes (animal hunts), public executions, and theatrical spectacles. It is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World and among the world's most visited tourist sites.

The Colosseum's construction was made possible by the spoils of the Jewish War (66-73 CE), including the sacking of the Temple in Jerusalem (70 CE) by Titus — Jewish slaves (according to tradition, up to 100,000) reportedly provided much of the construction labor. The structure's concrete and stone construction, its sophisticated seating stratification (different sections for senators, knights, plebeians, and women), its underground hypogeum (animal and gladiator storage tunnels), and its awning system (velarium) for shade demonstrate extraordinary Roman engineering.

The gladiatorial games held at the Colosseum were fundamental to Roman cultural life — not merely entertainment but civic ritual, imperial propaganda, and the expression of Roman values around courage, death, and social hierarchy. The games continued for centuries before gradually declining in the 5th century CE. Medieval Rome used the Colosseum as a fortress, then a quarry for building material — much of the original marble and travertine was removed for medieval church and palace construction. It became a Christian pilgrimage site associated with early Christian martyrdom (though the historical evidence for mass Christian martyrdom there is debated).

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Roman Colosseum — the largest ancient amphitheater, built with Jewish War spoils, venue of gladiatorial combat for centuries, and one of the world's most recognized monuments — is among the most historically significant structures in human history, embodying Roman imperial civilization, engineering, and cultural values.
